transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, I suppose the main thing is I’ve noticed I can’t seem to stay seated when I’m meant to. Like in staff meetings, or even at dinner, everyone else is sitting there and I’ll suddenly get up to refill coffee, or check a handout, or wander to the back of the room. It feels like I need to do something, even though when I think about it, it’s not really urgent.

I’m a teacher, so meetings are part of life, unfortunately—sorry, that’s not really the point—but it’s been happening enough that I’ve started wondering why I keep doing it.
Do you have any recurring thoughts that you can't seem to get out of your head?

I don’t think so… not in the way you mean, anyway. I mean, I’ll have a lot of things bouncing around in my head, especially school things—marking, emails, who needs what form signed—but I wouldn’t say it’s one thought that gets stuck and won’t leave.

Though now I’m wondering if you mean worries? Because I can get preoccupied with little practical things, like whether I remembered to lock the classroom cupboard, but then I’ll usually move on to something else. Sorry, I’m not sure if I’m answering that properly.
Do you often feel anxious or on edge?

Anxious… I don’t know, not especially? I mean, everyone at school is a bit on edge at certain times—exam season, inspections, when the photocopier jams five minutes before a lesson, which is practically a weekly event—but I wouldn’t say I walk around feeling anxious all the time.

I can get a bit keyed up, I suppose, but I’m not sure if that’s anxiety or just being busy. What do you mean by “on edge,” exactly?
Do you feel like you have to do things in a certain way or repeat certain actions?

Not really, I don’t think so. I mean, I have routines, like most teachers do—if you don’t have some sort of system, the whole day falls apart, especially with thirty pupils all needing something at once—but I wouldn’t say I have to do things a certain way or repeat things.

I might double-check I’ve got my keys or my register, but that feels more like being practical than anything. Sorry, I’ve gone off a bit. No, I haven’t noticed any repeating actions like that.
Do you often act on impulse without thinking things through?

Yes, I suppose I do—though not in a dramatic way. It’s more in conversations. Like at book club, or curriculum meetings at school, I’ll suddenly jump in before someone’s actually finished what they’re saying because the answer is already there in my head and out it comes.

It’s embarrassing sometimes, because I don’t mean to be rude. I’ll think, “Oh, for goodness’ sake, let them finish,” but by then I’ve already said it. It happens more when I’m interested in the topic, actually—if we’re discussing a novel or planning a scheme of work, I get carried along with it.
Do you often find yourself fidgeting with your hands or feet when you're sitting still?

Yes, I do, actually. Not constantly, but enough that I notice it. If I’m sitting at my desk marking essays, I’ll realise my foot’s been tapping away for ages, or I’m clicking my pen without thinking—which is dreadful if someone else is in the room, because it’s the sort of thing that would drive me mad if a pupil were doing it.

And in church, when I’m meant to be sitting still and listening properly, I’ll find I’m shifting about in the pew or moving my feet, and then I sort of tell myself, “Right, settle down.” It’s not deliberate, it just seems to happen when I’m sitting still for too long.
Are these behaviors, like getting up during meetings or fidgeting, causing problems for you at work or in your relationships with others?

Yes… I think it has started to, a bit. Not in a catastrophic way, but people do lose patience with me sometimes, especially in meetings at work. I can see it on their faces when I’ve jumped in again or when I’m shifting about instead of just sitting quietly.

And at book club too, which sounds silly, because that’s meant to be enjoyable—we were discussing a novel last month and I kept coming in too quickly, and afterwards I went home feeling embarrassed rather than, you know, part of things. Connected, I suppose. Same with people in the community sometimes. I don’t mean any harm, but I can leave feeling I’ve irritated everyone.
Do you feel like these behaviors are affecting your overall well-being or causing you a lot of distress?

Yes, I think it does, though I almost feel silly saying that because it’s not as if anything dreadful has happened. But it does wear on me.

It’s more the after-effect, really. I’ll come away from a staff meeting or book club thinking, “Why did I say that like that?” or “Why couldn’t I just wait?” And then I feel embarrassed, and a bit separate from people, instead of feeling I’ve joined in properly. People do lose patience with me sometimes — not always openly, but you can tell, can’t you?

It’s affected things at work and in the community a bit, I’d say. I used to really enjoy those sorts of discussions, and I still do, but now I sometimes dread that I’ll irritate everyone again.
Do you often struggle to follow through on instructions or finish tasks, such as lesson plans or grading assignments?

I’m not sure, actually. I mean, with lesson plans and marking, I do finish them because one has to, don’t you? The pupils are coming in whether I’m ready or not, and the essays can’t mark themselves—more’s the pity.

I suppose I can get a bit waylaid, but I don’t know if it’s more than anyone else. Sometimes I’ll sit down to do one thing and end up sorting a pile of papers or remembering I need to email someone about a school trip—well, not even a trip, more like one of those assemblies we all get roped into—and then I think, “What was I meant to be doing?”

But I wouldn’t want to say I often don’t follow through on instructions. I’m not sure that’s the main thing, really.
Do you often find yourself easily distracted by things around you?

I’m not sure, really. I mean, I notice things going on around me — in a classroom you rather have to, don’t you? A child rummaging in a bag, someone at the window, the radiator making that dreadful clanking noise we still haven’t had fixed.

But whether I’m more distracted than other people… I don’t know. I haven’t particularly thought of it that way. Sometimes I’ll lose my thread if there’s a lot happening, but then in school there always is a lot happening. Even the corridors have their own weather, almost — noise, coats everywhere, someone needing a form signed.

So… I’m not sure I’d say it’s a big thing I’ve noticed, no.
Do you often find yourself talking more than others in social situations?

Yes… I think I do, actually. Not all the time, but I’ve noticed it particularly in the Spanish department, or at the cultural centre, where we’ll be discussing something quite ordinary and I somehow end up giving three examples when one would have done.

It’s funny, because I don’t set out to dominate anything. I just get caught up — like if we’re talking about a film screening, I’ll start mentioning the director, and then something about an article I read, and then a student who once said something relevant, and by then I can see someone glancing at their watch or doing that polite little “right, anyway” face.

And then afterwards I feel embarrassed. I think, “Why didn’t I just stop sooner?” So yes, I suppose I can take over a conversation more than I mean to.
Do you think your difficulty staying seated and fidgeting is more related to feeling restless or having trouble paying attention?

I think it’s more a restlessness thing, probably. It’s not always that I’ve stopped listening exactly — though I suppose if I’m walking to the back of the room, I’m not fully sitting with it, am I?

It’s more that in meetings, or even at dinner when everyone else is perfectly settled, I suddenly feel I ought to get up and do something. Refill the coffee, check whether there are enough handouts, move something at the side of the room… and then afterwards I think, “Was that actually necessary?” Usually it wasn’t urgent at all.

It’s a bit embarrassing, really, because other people can just stay put, and I’m up and down like I’m hosting a village fête.
Do you often make impulsive decisions without fully considering the consequences?

I’m not sure I’d call them impulsive decisions, exactly. I mean, I can decide things rather quickly sometimes — in a staffroom sort of way, you know, “Yes, let’s move that lesson to Thursday,” or “Oh, I’ll volunteer for that,” and then later I remember my diary is already full of tiny little traps.

But serious decisions… I don’t think I’m reckless. I’m not off buying cars or booking flights to Peru on a whim — though Peru would be wonderful, wouldn’t it, all those textiles and the mountains. We did a unit once where a student brought in something her grandmother had woven, and I remember thinking—

Sorry, I’m wandering. I suppose I haven’t really noticed myself making big decisions without thinking through the consequences. Smaller things, perhaps, but I don’t know that it’s a major problem.
Do you think you have more trouble with staying focused on tasks or with sitting still and being patient?

I think it’s more the sitting still and being patient side of it. I can focus, at least sometimes, if I’m properly engaged, but what brought me in really was this business of getting up when everyone else is seated.

In meetings I’ll suddenly think, “Oh, I should refill the coffee,” or “I’d better check those handouts,” and I’m halfway out of my chair before I’ve really considered whether it needs doing. Or at dinner, I’ll pop up to move something or fetch something, and everyone else is just… calmly sitting there like normal adults.

Sometimes I’ll walk to the back of the room as if there’s a purpose, but there often isn’t anything urgent. It’s more like I can’t quite remain planted. Then afterwards I feel a bit silly, because it probably could have waited.
Do you think your mind often wanders off when you're supposed to be listening to someone or doing a task?

I’m not sure, really. I mean, everyone’s mind wanders sometimes, doesn’t it? Especially if someone is explaining a timetable change for the third time and there’s a poster peeling off the wall behind them — I always notice things like that.

But whether it’s often… I don’t know. I haven’t particularly noticed it as the main thing. I can usually follow someone if I’m trying to, though I might drift a little and then come back. It’s hard to judge, isn’t it, because you only notice once you’ve already wandered.
Do you think your difficulty with sitting still and fidgeting is more closely related to feeling overly energetic or to having trouble paying attention to what's going on around you?

I think it’s more like an excess of energy in my body than not paying attention, if that makes sense. I can be listening, but my foot is going under the desk like a sewing machine.

When I’m grading essays at my desk, for instance, I’ll catch myself tapping my foot or clicking my pen, and then I suddenly think, “Oh, stop that, that’s probably maddening.” Or in church, which is possibly the worst place for it because everything is so quiet, I’ll realise I’ve been shifting about in the pew and have to tell myself to sit properly.

It’s not usually because I don’t know what’s happening around me. It’s more that I have to keep reminding my body to settle down.
Have you always been this way, even as a child?

Yes, I think so. I mean, my mother certainly thought so. She used to joke that before I was ten I’d worn a little path between my desk and the pencil sharpener, because I was up and down so much.

And my school reports — funny, I kept some of them for years in a box with old certificates and, oddly, a programme from a school play I wasn’t even in — they’d say things like I was bright, but I couldn’t stay in my seat or wait my turn. So yes, looking back, it was there when I was a girl too.
Have you ever been unable to work or participate in social activities because of your difficulty staying seated or controlling your impulses?

Not unable to work, exactly — I still turn up, I still do what I’m meant to do. But it has started to affect things, socially and at work.

Meetings are the worst. I’ll shift in my chair or jump in too quickly, and I can see people getting that look, you know, the “please just wait” look. We have this one meeting room with dreadful chairs — though honestly every school seems to buy chairs designed by someone who hates spines — but anyway, I leave feeling embarrassed.

And book club too. I like going, I really do, but sometimes I talk too soon or can’t quite sit through the longer discussions, and people lose patience. So I’m not exactly stopped from participating, but I come away feeling more ashamed than connected, which rather defeats the point of going.
Were you more restless or fidgety as a child compared to your peers?

Yes, I think I was. It’s a bit hard to compare properly, because children are children, aren’t they — they all wriggle about to some extent. But even as a girl, it was commented on.

My report cards used to say I was bright, which was always the nice bit my mother liked to point out, but then there’d be the “however” — couldn’t stay in my seat, couldn’t wait my turn, that sort of thing. And my mother used to joke that before I was ten I’d practically worn a path between my desk and the pencil sharpener. I can still picture those old metal sharpeners on the wall, actually. So yes, I suppose compared with the other girls, I was noticeably more restless.

When I’m grading essays at my desk, for instance, I’ll catch myself tapping my foot or clicking my pen, and then I suddenly think, “Oh, stop that, that’s probably maddening.” Or in church, which is possibly the worst place for it because everything is so quiet, I’ll realise I’ve been shifting about in the pew and have to tell myself to sit properly.

It’s not usually because I don’t know what’s happening around me. It’s more that I have to keep reminding my body to settle down.

doctor.intent: determine if symptoms have been present since childhood
doctor.question: Have you always been this way, even as a child?

target_item.name: Additional Requirement 1
target_item.manifestation: Even as a girl, my report cards said I was bright but could not stay in my seat or wait my turn, and my mother used to joke that I wore a path between my desk and the pencil sharpener before I was ten.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether these symptoms have been present since childhood, which directly relates to onset before age 12.

patient.answer:
Yes, I think so. I mean, my mother certainly thought so. She used to joke that before I was ten I’d worn a little path between my desk and the pencil sharpener, because I was up and down so much.

And my school reports — funny, I kept some of them for years in a box with old certificates and, oddly, a programme from a school play I wasn’t even in — they’d say things like I was bright, but I couldn’t stay in my seat or wait my turn. So yes, looking back, it was there when I was a girl too.

doctor.intent: determine if the patient's symptoms have caused significant impairment in social or occupational functioning
doctor.question: Have you ever been unable to work or participate in social activities because of your difficulty staying seated or controlling your impulses?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: It has started to affect my relationships at work and in my community because people lose patience with me in meetings and book club, and I leave feeling embarrassed instead of connected.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the symptoms interfere with work or social participation, which is about functional impairment.

patient.answer:
Not unable to work, exactly — I still turn up, I still do what I’m meant to do. But it has started to affect things, socially and at work.

Meetings are the worst. I’ll shift in my chair or jump in too quickly, and I can see people getting that look, you know, the “please just wait” look. We have this one meeting room with dreadful chairs — though honestly every school seems to buy chairs designed by someone who hates spines — but anyway, I leave feeling embarrassed.

And book club too. I like going, I really do, but sometimes I talk too soon or can’t quite sit through the longer discussions, and people lose patience. So I’m not exactly stopped from participating, but I come away feeling more ashamed than connected, which rather defeats the point of going.

doctor.intent: Determine if symptoms have been present since childhood to differentiate between F90.0 and F90.8
doctor.question: Were you more restless or fidgety as a child compared to your peers?

target_item.name: Additional Requirement 1
target_item.manifestation: Even as a girl, my report cards said I was bright but could not stay in my seat or wait my turn, and my mother used to joke that I wore a path between my desk and the pencil sharpener before I was ten.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the restlessness or fidgetiness was present in childhood, which directly relates to onset before age 12.

patient.answer:
Yes, I think I was. It’s a bit hard to compare properly, because children are children, aren’t they — they all wriggle about to some extent. But even as a girl, it was commented on.

My report cards used to say I was bright, which was always the nice bit my mother liked to point out, but then there’d be the “however” — couldn’t stay in my seat, couldn’t wait my turn, that sort of thing. And my mother used to joke that before I was ten I’d practically worn a path between my desk and the pencil sharpener. I can still picture those old metal sharpeners on the wall, actually. So yes, I suppose compared with the other girls, I was noticeably more restless.
